A type conversion performed automatically as part of an operation.
A type conversion requested directly by program code.
A comparison that checks type and value without coercing operands.
A comparison that can convert operands before deciding whether they are equal.
A value that behaves like true when used as a condition.
A value that behaves like false when used as a condition.
A numeric value representing an invalid or unrepresentable numeric result.
The conversion of a value to the true or false primitive.
A relationship in which two references point to the same object value.
A value or expression that an operator acts upon.
A built-in comparison that distinguishes signed zero and treats NaN as equal to itself.

Both variables refer to the same object identity.

questions.question: Why is strict equality often preferred over loose equality?
keyPoints: Strict equality does not coerce types
questions.modelAnswer: Strict equality compares without converting operand types, which makes the comparison's assumptions clearer. Loose equality can be useful only when its coercion behavior is intentional and well understood.

questions.question: What kinds of values are falsy, and why should code avoid confusing falsy with missing?
keyPoints: Falsy values include false, zero, empty string, null, undefined, and NaN
Empty arrays and objects are truthy
questions.modelAnswer: Falsy values include false, zero, the empty string, null, undefined, and NaN; empty arrays and objects are truthy. A valid value such as zero can be falsy, so presence checks should not rely on truthiness alone.

questions.question: Why should Number.isNaN be used instead of comparing a value with NaN?
keyPoints: NaN is unequal to itself under equality operators
Number.isNaN tests the actual numeric NaN value
Input conversion can be checked separately
questions.modelAnswer: NaN is not equal to itself, so a comparison such as value === NaN is always false. Number.isNaN checks specifically for the numeric NaN value without coercing an unrelated input.
